statement: To construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome.
heath_proof: Let ABCD, CBEF, two planes of the aforesaid cube at right angles to one another, be set out, let the sides AB, BC, CD, DA, EF, EB, FC be bisected at G, H, K, L, M, N, O respectively, let GK, HL, MH, NO be joined, let the straight lines NP, PO, HQ be cut in extreme and mean ratio at the points R, S, T respectively, and let RP, PS, TQ be their greater segments; from the points R, S, T let RU, SV, TW be set up at right angles to the planes of the cube towards the outside of the cube, let them be made equal to RP, PS, TQ, and let UB, BW, WC, CV, VU be joined. I say that the pentagon UBWCV is equilateral, and in one plane, and is further equiangular. For let RB, SB, VB be joined. Then, since the straight line NP has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at R, and RP is the greater segment, therefore the squares on PN, NR are triple of the square on RP. [XIII. 4] But PN is equal to NB, and PR to RU; therefore the squares on BN, NR are triple of the square on RU. But the square on BR is equal to the squares on BN, NR; [I. 47] therefore the square on BR is triple of the square on RU; hence the squares on BR, RU are quadruple of the square on RU. But the square on BU is equal to the squares on BR, RU; therefore the square on BU is quadruple of the square on RU; therefore BU is double of RU. But VU is also double of UR, inasmuch as SR is also double of PR, that is, of RU; therefore BU is equal to UV. Similarly it can be proved that each of the straight lines BW, WC, CV is also equal to each of the straight lines BU, UV. Therefore the pentagon BUVCW is equilateral. I say next that it is also in one plane. For let PX be drawn from P parallel to each of the straight lines RU, SV and towards the outside of the cube, and let XH, HW be joined; I say that XHW is a straight line. For, since HQ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at T, and QT is its greater segment, therefore, as HQ is to QT, so is QT to TH. But HQ is equal to HP, and QT to each of the straight lines TW, PX; therefore, as HP is to PX, so is WT to TH. And HP is parallel to TW, for each of them is at right angles to the plane BD; [XI. 6] and TH is parallel to PX, for each of them is at right angles to the plane BF. [id.] But if two triangles, as XPH, HTW, which have two sides proportional to two sides be placed together at one angle so that their corresponding sides are also parallel, the remaining straight lines will be in a straight line; [VI. 32] therefore XH is in a straight line with HW. But every straight line is in one plane; [XI. 1] therefore the pentagon UBWCV is in one plane. I say next that it is also equiangular. For, since the straight line NP has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at R, and PR is the greater segment, while PR is equal to PS, therefore NS has also been cut in extreme and mean ratio at P, and NP is the greater segment; [XIII. 5] therefore the squares on NS, SP are triple of the square on NP. [XIII. 4] But NP is equal to NB, and PS to SV; therefore the squares on NS, SV are triple of the square on NB; hence the squares on VS, SN, NB are quadruple of the square on NB. But the square on SB is equal to the squares on SN, NB; therefore the squares on BS, SV, that is, the square on BV —for the angle VSB is right—is quadruple of the square on NB; therefore VB is double of BN. But BC is also double of BN; therefore BV is equal to BC. And, since the two sides BU, UV are equal to the two sides BW, WC, and the base BV is equal to the base BC, therefore the angle BUV is equal to the angle BWC. [I. 8] Similarly we can prove that the angle UVC is also equal to the angle BWC; therefore the three angles BWC, BUV, UVC are equal to one another. But if in an equilateral pentagon three angles are equal to one another, the pentagon will be equiangular, [XIII. 7] therefore the pentagon BUVCW is equiangular. And it was also proved equilateral; therefore the pentagon BUVCW is equilateral and equiangular, and it is on one side BC of the cube. Therefore, if we make the same construction in the case of each of the twelve sides of the cube, a solid figure will have been constructed which is contained by twelve equilateral and equiangular pentagons, and which is called a dodecahedron. It is then required to comprehend it in the given sphere, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome. For let XP be produced, and let the produced straight line be XZ; therefore PZ meets the diameter of the cube, and they bisect one another, for this has been proved in the last theorem but one of the eleventh book. [XI. 38] Let them cut at Z; therefore Z is the centre of the sphere which comprehends the cube, and ZP is half of the side of the cube. Let UZ be joined. Now, since the straight line NS has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at P, and NP is its greater segment, therefore the squares on NS, SP are triple of the square on NP. [XIII. 4] But NS is equal to XZ, inasmuch as NP is also equal to PZ, and XP to PS. But further PS is also equal to XU, since it is also equal to RP; therefore the squares on ZX, XU are triple of the square on NP. But the square on UZ is equal to the squares on ZX, XU; therefore the square on UZ is triple of the square on NP. But the square on the radius of the sphere which comprehends the cube is also triple of the square on the half of the side of the cube, for it has previously been shown how to construct a cube and comprehend it in a sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube. [XIII. 15] But, if whole is so related to whole, so is half to half also; and NP is half of the side of the cube; therefore UZ is equal to the radius of the sphere which comprehends the cube. And Z is the centre of the sphere which comprehends the cube; therefore the point U is on the surface of the sphere. Similarly we can prove that each of the remaining angles of the dodecahedron is also on the surface of the sphere; therefore the dodecahedron has been comprehended in the given sphere. I say next that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome. For since, when NP has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, RP is the greater segment, and, when PO has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, PS is the greater segment, therefore, when the whole NO is cut in extreme and mean ratio, RS is the greater segment. [Thus, since, as NP is to PR, so is PR to RN, the same is true of the doubles also, for parts have the same ratio as their equimultiples; [V. 15] therefore as NO is to RS, so is RS to the sum of NR, SO. But NO is greater than RS; therefore RS is also greater than the sum of NR, SO; therefore NO has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and RS is its greater segment.] But RS is equal to UV; therefore, when NO is cut in extreme and mean ratio, UV is the greater segment. And, since the diameter of the sphere is rational, and the square on it is triple of the square on the side of the cube, therefore NO, being a side of the cube, is rational. [But if a rational line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, each of the segments is an irrational apotome.] Therefore UV, being a side of the dodecahedron, is an irrational apotome. [XIII. 6]
ai_proof_text:
13.17
**Statement:** To construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome.

**Step 1.** Setting out. Let the diameter of the given sphere be taken as the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3). By 13.15 construct a cube comprehended in this sphere; then the diameter of the cube is a diameter of the sphere and the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube (13.15). The cube is contained by six equal squares (D11.25); let ABCD and CBEF be two of its faces with common side BC, so that they are squares (D1.22) whose planes are at right angles to one another.

**Step 2.** Bisect AB, BC, CD, DA, EF, EB, FC at G, H, K, L, M, N, O (1.10) and join GK, HL, MH, NO (P1). Since N, O bisect the equal and parallel sides EB, FC, the lines NB, OC are equal and parallel, so NO is equal and parallel to BC (1.33); similarly MH is equal and parallel to EB, GK to BC, and HL to AB. Let MH, NO meet at P and GK, HL at Q. Then NBHP, PHCO, BHQG are parallelograms, so NP = BH, PO = HC, HQ = BG (1.34). Since BH, HC, BG, BN, OC are halves of equal sides of the cube, NP = PO = HQ = NB = OC = BH = HC.

**Step 3.** Cut NP in extreme and mean ratio at R with RP the greater segment (6.30), so that NP : RP = RP : RN (D6.3). Cut off PS = RP on PO and QT = RP on QH (1.3). Since PO = NP and HQ = NP, the remainders SO and TH are each equal to NR (CN3). Hence PO : PS = NP : RP = RP : RN = PS : SO (5.7, 5.11), so PO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at S with PS the greater segment (D6.3); likewise HQ : QT = QT : TH, so HQ is cut in extreme and mean ratio at T with QT the greater segment.

**Step 4.** From R and S set up RU, SV at right angles to the plane CBEF, and from T set up TW at right angles to the plane ABCD, all on the outside of the cube (11.12), and make RU = SV = TW = RP (1.3). Join UB, BW, WC, CV, VU (P1).

**Step 5.** Since NO is parallel to BC and NB falls on them, the angles BNO, NBC together equal two right angles (1.29); angle NBC is right (D1.22), so angle BNR is right. Hence BR² = BN² + NR² (1.47).

**Step 6.** Since NP is cut in extreme and mean ratio at R with RP the greater segment, NP² + NR² = 3·RP² (13.4). But NP = NB and RP = RU; therefore BN² + NR² = 3·RU², that is, BR² = 3·RU² (Step 5, CN1).

**Step 7.** Since RU is at right angles to the plane CBEF and RB lies in that plane, angle URB is right (D11.3); hence BU² = BR² + RU² = 3·RU² + RU² = 4·RU² (1.47, CN2).

**Step 8.** RU and SV are both at right angles to the plane CBEF, so they are parallel (11.6); being also equal, the line UV joining their ends is equal and parallel to RS (1.33). Now RS = RP + PS = 2·RP = 2·RU, so UV = 2·RU and UV² = 4·RU² (2.4). Therefore BU² = UV² (CN1), and BU = UV.

**Step 9.** Similarly for the other sides. PO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at S with PS the greater, so PO² + OS² = 3·PS² (13.4); angle COS is right (1.29, as in Step 5) so CS² = CO² + OS² = 3·SV² (1.47, since CO = PO, SV = PS); angle VSC is right (D11.3), so CV² = CS² + SV² = 4·SV² = UV². Again HQ is cut in extreme and mean ratio at T with QT the greater, so HQ² + HT² = 3·QT² (13.4); HL is parallel to AB so angle BHT is right (1.29) and BT² = BH² + HT² = 3·TW² (1.47, since BH = HQ, TW = QT); angle WTB is right (D11.3), so BW² = BT² + TW² = 4·TW² = UV²; in the same way CW² = CH² + HT² + TW² = 4·TW² = UV². Hence UB = BW = WC = CV = VU, and the pentagon UBWCV is equilateral.

**Step 10.** Next, it lies in one plane. From P set up PX at right angles to the plane CBEF on the outside (11.12) and make PX = RP (1.3). PX is parallel to RU (11.6) and equal to it, so UX is equal and parallel to RP (1.33); similarly XV is equal and parallel to PS. Thus UX and XV both pass through X and are parallel to NO; if they were two distinct straight lines they would be parallel to one another (1.30) yet meet at X, contrary to D1.23; hence UXV is one straight line and X lies on UV. Also UV is parallel to NO (Step 8) and NO to BC, these not all lying in one plane, so UV is parallel to BC (11.9).

**Step 11.** Join XH and HW (P1). Since MH is parallel to EB and EB is at right angles to BC, MH is at right angles to BC (1.29); the planes ABCD, CBEF are at right angles with common section BC, so HP, lying in the plane CBEF at right angles to BC, is at right angles to the plane ABCD (D11.4). TW is also at right angles to the plane ABCD, so HP is parallel to TW (11.6). Likewise HL is parallel to AB and AB is at right angles to BC, so HT, lying in the plane ABCD at right angles to BC, is at right angles to the plane CBEF (1.29, D11.4); PX is at right angles to the same plane, so HT is parallel to PX (11.6).

**Step 12.** By Step 3, HQ : QT = QT : TH. But HQ = HP and QT = TW = PX; hence HP : PX = PX : TH (5.7), and inversely PX : HP = TH : PX, that is, XP : PH = HT : TW (5.7). Thus the triangles XPH and HTW have the two sides XP, PH proportional to the two sides HT, TW, they are placed together at the point H, and the corresponding sides are parallel (XP to HT, PH to TW, Step 11). Therefore XH is in a straight line with HW (6.32).

**Step 13.** UV and BC are parallel (Step 10) and so lie in one plane (D1.23). X is on UV and H is on BC, so the straight line XH lies in the plane of the parallels UV, BC (11.7). W lies on XH produced (Step 12), and a straight line cannot be partly in a plane and partly outside it (11.1); therefore W lies in that plane. Hence U, B, W, C, V all lie in one plane.

**Step 14.** Next, it is equiangular. Join BV (P1). Since NP is cut in extreme and mean ratio at R with RP the greater segment, and PS equal to RP has been added to it, the whole NS is cut in extreme and mean ratio at P with NP the greater segment (13.5); hence NS² + SP² = 3·NP² (13.4). Angle BNS is right (Step 5), so BS² = BN² + NS² (1.47); angle VSB is right (D11.3), so BV² = BS² + SV² = BN² + NS² + SP² = NP² + 3·NP² = 4·NP² (1.47, since BN = NP and SV = SP). But BC = 2·BH = 2·NP, so BC² = 4·NP² (2.4). Therefore BV² = BC² and BV = BC.

**Step 15.** Join UC (P1). Since PO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at S with PS the greater segment, and PR equal to PS has been added, RO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at P with PO the greater segment (13.5); hence RO² + RP² = 3·PO² (13.4). Angle COR is right (Step 9), so CR² = CO² + RO² (1.47); angle URC is right (D11.3), so UC² = CR² + RU² = CO² + RO² + RP² = PO² + 3·PO² = 4·PO² = BC² (1.47, 2.4, since CO = PO, RU = RP, BC = 2·PO). Therefore UC = BC.

**Step 16.** In the triangles BUV, BWC the sides BU = BW, UV = WC and the bases BV = BC; therefore angle BUV = angle BWC (1.8). In the triangles CVU, CWB the sides VU = WB, VC = WC and the bases CU = CB; therefore angle UVC = angle BWC (1.8). Thus the three angles BUV, BWC, UVC of the equilateral pentagon UBWCV are equal to one another; hence the pentagon is equiangular (13.7). So UBWCV is an equilateral and equiangular pentagon standing on the edge BC of the cube.

**Step 17.** Making the same construction on each of the twelve edges of the cube, we obtain a solid figure contained by twelve equal, equilateral and equiangular pentagons, which is a dodecahedron (D11.28). This is the required construction.

**Step 18.** Next, it is comprehended in the given sphere. Produce XP through P into the cube (P2). Since P is the centre of the face CBEF and PX is at right angles to that face, the line so produced is the common section of the two planes drawn through the points of bisection of the sides of the cube; hence it meets the diameter of the cube at a point Z at which the two bisect one another (11.38). Thus Z is the middle point of the diameter of the cube, which is a diameter of the sphere (Step 1, D11.17), so Z is the centre of the sphere (D11.16); and PZ, being half of the common section, which is equal to the side of the cube, is equal to half the side, that is, PZ = NP. Join UZ (P1).

**Step 19.** XZ = XP + PZ = PS + NP = NS (CN2), and XU = RP = SP (Step 10). Since UX is parallel to PS and XP falls on them, the angles SPX, PXU together equal two right angles (1.29); angle SPX is right (D11.3), so angle UXZ is right. Hence UZ² = XU² + XZ² = SP² + NS² = 3·NP² = 3·PZ² (1.47, Step 14, CN1).

**Step 20.** The side of the cube is 2·PZ, so the square on it is 4·PZ² (2.4); the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of this (13.15), namely 12·PZ². The diameter is double of the semidiameter, so the square on the diameter is four times the square on the semidiameter (2.4); hence the square on the semidiameter is 3·PZ² (CN1). Therefore UZ² equals the square on the semidiameter and UZ equals the semidiameter of the sphere. Since Z is the centre, U lies on the surface of the sphere (D11.14, D11.16). Similarly each of the remaining vertices of the dodecahedron lies on the surface; hence the dodecahedron is comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 21.** Finally, the side is an apotome. The square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side BC of the cube (13.15), so the square on BC has to the square on the diameter the ratio 1 : 3, which a number has to a number; hence these squares are commensurable (10.6). The square on the diameter is rational (D10.1.4), so BC is commensurable in square with the assigned rational line (D10.1.2) and is therefore rational (D10.1.3). NO = BC (Step 2), so NO is rational.

**Step 22.** NO = 2·NP, RS = RP + PS = 2·RP, and NR + SO = 2·NR (Step 3). Since NP : RP = RP : RN (Step 3), and parts have the same ratio as their equimultiples, NO : RS = NP : RP and RS : (NR + SO) = RP : NR (5.15); therefore NO : RS = RS : (NR + SO) (5.11).

**Step 23.** Cut off NY = RS from NO (1.3); then YO = NO − NY = NR + SO (CN3), so NO : NY = NY : YO (Step 22). Since NO is greater than NY, NY is greater than YO (5.14); hence NO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at Y with NY the greater segment (D6.3). NO is rational (Step 21), so its segment NY is the irrational straight line called apotome (13.6). But NY = RS = UV (Step 8), a side of the dodecahedron. Therefore the side of the dodecahedron is an apotome.

**Step 24.** Therefore a dodecahedron has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere, and its side has been proved to be the irrational straight line called apotome. Q.E.F.
